name: Ngala
confidence_why: The only remark on Ngala prosody is Migeod's 1922 note, taken from two very old rememberers of an already dying Kotoko variety, that the last syllable "sometimes" carried emphasis in a rising tone, which cannot be told apart from tone or phrase-final intonation, and Gravina 2014 says nothing about Ngala or about stress, so no word-stress system can be stated.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened at p. 276 (= JRAI 52 p. 241, running head 'F. W. H. Migeod.—Ngala, and its Dead Language. 241') and the saved page scan. The 'NOTE' after the pronoun table reads exactly: 'As to accent, I sometimes found the last syllable of a word had an emphasis on it, and it was in a rising tone.' (page scan checked; the text has scanned noise '[ sometimes', 'eyllable' but the printed page matches the quote verbatim). It is the only prosodic remark in the article; the rest of the Note concerns Barth's vs Migeod's transcriptions (N/L, Sh/Th, H/A, Kanuri numerals). Read pp. 230-241 (PDF 265-276): identity confirmed as ngal1301 — Ngala town '28 miles north-north-east of Dikwa on the south side of Lak…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Migeod reports only an impression: in some words the final syllable carried emphasis (prominence) together with a rising pitch. He states no rule, no contrast, and gives no marked examples; the observation is consistent with final-syllable prominence but equally with citation-form final rising intonation on words elicited one by one from two elderly rememberers. If forced onto the fixed list the nearest label would be fixed: final syllable (low confidence).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the hedge 'sometimes' itself implies the emphasis was not found on every word.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated words elicited in citation form (a 'list' called out rapidly by two old men who were the last rememberers, p. 234); the wordlist pp. 236-241 shows no accent marks. Language already moribund in 1922 (present language of the town Kanuri).
new_statements.identity_note: Ngala of Lake Chad = the extinct Kotoko (Central Chadic) language of Ngala town, Borno State, Nigeria, called 'Sso/So' in the German sources; documented only by Barth (1850s wordlist, printed in Benton 1912), von Duisburg 1914 and Migeod 1922 (two elderly rememberers, Ladan Braima and Mahman Tahir). Migeod 1922: 234 says it 'was related to the Makari farther east', i.e. Mpade (mpad1242); Glottolog treats it as a distinct language equidistant from Mpade and Malgbe (ISO mxf). The quoted statement is about ngal1301 itself, not a proxy variety.

sources.note: p. 241, closing 'Note' after the wordlist and pronoun table: 'As to accent, I sometimes found the last syllable of a word had an emphasis on it, and it was in a rising tone.' The only prosodic remark; the wordlist (pp. 236-241) carries no accent marks (only a few circumflexes on vowels). Data from two very old rememberers (Ladan Braima, Mahman Tahir) at Ngala in 1922, p. 234: 'The old language of Ngala was related to the Makari farther east. Only two old men and one woman are left who know it.'

tone.quote: Der Akut (' ) bedeutet bei Zitaten von eingeborenen Wörtern und Namen der älteren Literatur im allgemeinen den Stärkeakzent, bei solchen aus neueren — besonders sprachlichen — Werken dagegen den Hochton, e. g. d. (Gravis, e. g. ä, = Tiefton ; meistens nicht bezeichnet, nur wenn im gleichen Wort vorhergehende Silbe hoch- oder mitteltonig. — ' = Mittelton, e. g. a. — Zirkumflex, e. g. ä, = fallender Ton. — Umgekehrter Zirkumflex, e. g. ä, = steigender Ton. — Das Tonzeichen gilt für alle folgenden unbezeichneten Silben mit. — â — ä etc. zeigt in älteren Werken gedehnte Vokale an.)
tone.locator: pp. 895-896 (digi-hub images 967-968), section 'Erläuterungen' before the bibliography
tone.translation: In citations of native words and names the acute generally denotes the stress accent when they come from the older literature, but the high tone when they come from newer, especially linguistic, works, e.g. á. (Grave, e.g. à, = low tone; mostly unmarked, only when a preceding syllable of the same word is high or mid. Macron = mid tone. Circumflex = falling tone. Inverted circumflex = rising tone. The tone mark holds for all following unmarked syllables. In older works â, ā etc. indicate lengthened vowels.)
tone.says: A historical-classificatory study (So vs. Ngala identity, Ngala = Kotoko dialect documented by Barth-Benton 1912, von Duisburg 1914, Migeod 1922, extinct by c. 1900 and replaced by Kanuri); it contains NO statement on tone or accent in Ngala and does not comment on Migeod's final-syllable 'rising tone' remark. The only tonal content is the notation key on pp. 895-896: an acute on forms quoted from older sources (Barth etc.) is to be read as stress accent, on forms from newer linguistic works as…

sources.note: The only other first-hand record of the language, taken when five speakers were still alive (Migeod 1922: 234 mentions 'the Germans some years ago took down a vocabulary'); German colonial-era word collections in MSOS often mark Betonung/Ton, so it may carry the only accent-marked data.

tone.summary: Says nothing about tone; a 1914 vocabulary of Sso from its last speaker at Ngala. Words carry unexplained acute accents (biskún, holá, kakántu); the one note given: breve = short vowel.

tone.says: Record only (pages not openable by automated download): the only mid-19th-century record of the language taken while it was in full use; Barth's vocabularies mark syllables with acute accents, which Sölken 1958: 895 instructs readers to take as stress accent, not tone; whether the Nghála column actually carries accent marks, and whether p. 137 says anything on pronunciation, is unverified. No tone analysis can be expected.
